Braille keyboard tutorial and practice
From zero to typing with ease: how to hold the phone, calibrate, every letter, numbers, punctuation and gestures, each lesson with its practice, and a field to try the real keyboard

What the braille keyboard is

The Tiresias braille keyboard lets you type in any app by touching the screen with six fingers, as on a Perkins brailler.

Each letter is a six-dot braille cell in two columns of three: on the left, from top to bottom, dots 1, 2 and 3; on the right, dots 4, 5 and 6. To type a letter, rest the fingers of its dots at the same time and lift them: when the last finger is lifted, the letter is typed and Tiresias says it. They do not need to land at exactly the same time; what matters is that all of them are down before you lift any.

The keyboard uses Spanish uncontracted braille (ONCE). If you have never written braille, do not worry: this tutorial starts from zero and almost every lesson has its practice.

While you practise or type, the Tiresias gestures do not work on the screen: the keyboard has its own, and two fingers up always gets you out. If something does not respond, press both volume keys together and everything goes back to normal.
How to hold the phone and where the dots are

There are two ways to hold it.

Screen away, the default: hold the phone sideways with both hands, the screen facing away from you, and the top of the phone, where the earpiece and the front camera are, in your left hand. Your fingers wrap around the phone and touch the screen; your thumbs stay at the back, holding it. With your left hand you type dots 1, 2 and 3: the index finger at the top is dot 1, the middle finger dot 2 and the ring finger at the bottom dot 3. With your right hand, the same: index dot 4, middle dot 5 and ring dot 6.

Tabletop: the phone lying sideways, screen up, with its top to your left. The six fingers in a row, as on a Perkins: from left to right, the ring, middle and index fingers of your left hand (dots 3, 2 and 1) and the index, middle and ring fingers of your right hand (dots 4, 5 and 6). To type like this, turn on «Mirrored dots» in the braille settings, or «Dots according to how you hold the phone» so Tiresias notices by itself.

The screen does not rotate while you type, so the dots stay where they are.

In the practice, touch different places with a single finger and Tiresias tells you which dot it is, until you find all six.
Calibrate: the dots where your fingers fall

Every hand is different. Calibrating tells Tiresias where you rest each finger, and from then on each touch counts as the nearest dot. It is the best thing to do before you start typing.

In the practice, hold the phone the way you will type and Tiresias asks for the dots one by one: touch dot 1, touch dot 2, and so on up to 6. Touch each one with a single finger, where it falls naturally. If two are too close together, it asks again. Two fingers up cancel it.

The calibration is saved separately for screen away and for tabletop. You can repeat it whenever you like, from here or from the keyboard menu, and remove it in the braille settings.
The first letters: a, b, c, d and e

The first ten letters only use the top and middle dots: 1, 2, 4 and 5. We start with five, and all of them have dot 1:

a: dot 1.
b: dots 1 and 2.
c: dots 1 and 4.
d: dots 1, 4 and 5.
e: dots 1 and 5.

In the practice, Tiresias asks for each letter with its dots; then comes a review in random order where it no longer says them, unless you make a mistake. If you get it wrong, it tells you what you typed and what was expected. Any gesture repeats the current request, and two fingers up leave the practice.
More letters: f, g, h, i and j

f: dots 1, 2 and 4.
g: dots 1, 2, 4 and 5.
h: dots 1, 2 and 5.
i: dots 2 and 4.
j: dots 2, 4 and 5.

I and j are the only ones in this series without dot 1. These ten letters, from a to j, are the basis of almost everything: the others are made by adding dots to them, and they are also the digits.
From k to t: add dot 3

The second series is the first one with dot 3 added:

k: dots 1 and 3 (a plus 3).
l: dots 1, 2 and 3.
m: dots 1, 3 and 4.
n: dots 1, 3, 4 and 5.
o: dots 1, 3 and 5.
p: dots 1, 2, 3 and 4.
q: dots 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5.
r: dots 1, 2, 3 and 5.
s: dots 2, 3 and 4.
t: dots 2, 3, 4 and 5.

If you remember the letter of the first series, you only need to add the finger of dot 3.
u, v, x, y, z, ñ and w

The third series adds dots 3 and 6 to the first one:

u: dots 1, 3 and 6.
v: dots 1, 2, 3 and 6.
x: dots 1, 3, 4 and 6.
y: dots 1, 3, 4, 5 and 6.
z: dots 1, 3, 5 and 6.

And two letters on their own:

ñ: dots 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6.
w: dots 2, 4, 5 and 6.
Accented vowels and ü

á: dots 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6.
é: dots 2, 3, 4 and 6.
í: dots 3 and 4.
ó: dots 3, 4 and 6.
ú: dots 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6.
ü: dots 1, 2, 5 and 6.

They do not look like their unaccented vowels: you have to learn them separately. Í and ó are the shortest.
Capitals and numbers

For a capital letter, first type the capital sign, dots 4 and 6, and then the letter: capital B is dots 4 and 6 and then 1 and 2. It only applies to the next letter.

For a number, first type the number sign, dots 3, 4, 5 and 6, and then the digits with the letters a to j: 1 is a, 2 b, 3 c, 4 d, 5 e, 6 f, 7 g, 8 h, 9 i and 0 j. The number sign applies to all the digits in a row, until a space or a letter outside a to j. So 25 is the number sign, b and e.

Each digit is spoken as you type it, and when you add the space after it Tiresias says the whole number: typing 2026 and a space you hear «two thousand twenty-six». Comma and full stop work inside a number (3.5).

In the braille settings you can turn on «Automatic capitals», which adds the capital by itself at the start of a sentence.
Punctuation

Almost all of them are in the lower part of the cell:

Full stop: dot 3.
Comma: dot 2.
Semicolon: dots 2 and 3.
Colon: dots 2 and 5.
Question mark: dots 2 and 6.
Exclamation mark: dots 2, 3 and 5.
Hyphen: dots 3 and 6.
Opening parenthesis: dots 1, 2 and 6; closing: dots 3, 4 and 5.
Quotation marks: dots 2, 3 and 6.
Apostrophe: dot 5.
Equals: dots 2, 3, 5 and 6.
Asterisk: dots 3 and 5.
Slash: dots 2, 5 and 6.
Underscore: dots 4, 5 and 6.

In braille, the question mark and the exclamation mark are the same sign for opening and closing. The keyboard decides by where you type it: at the start (at the beginning, after a space or a parenthesis) it types ¿ and ¡; after a word, ? and !.

The practice asks for the first seven and a review.
Gestures: space, delete, Enter and more

Besides the dots, the keyboard has gestures: sliding one, two or three fingers in a direction. Directions are yours, with the phone held for typing: right means towards your right. To count as a gesture, move your finger at least one centimetre; if you move it less, it is a dot.

By default:

One finger right: space.
One finger left: delete the previous letter.
Two fingers left: delete the word.
Two fingers down: Enter, or whatever the field asks for (send, search, next). In messaging apps, it presses Send.
One finger up: the keyboard menu.
One finger down: hide the keyboard without sending anything. If Tiresias has just said there are mention suggestions (after typing an at sign in WhatsApp), the same gesture opens them.
Two fingers right: dictate with your voice.
Three fingers left or right: move the cursor through the text, saying what it passes.
Three fingers down: change what the cursor moves by (character, word or line).
Two fingers up: back to the keyboard you had before (and out of the practices).
Three fingers up: the screen reader menu (the curtain, the time, the voice…).

All of them can be changed in «Braille keyboard gestures», in the braille settings; the practice uses the ones you have set.
The keyboard menu

One finger up opens the keyboard menu: emoji, search for an emoji, clipboard, suggestions (if you are mentioning someone), dictation, read everything typed, Editing, delete the word, calibrate, remove the calibration, lock the orientation, screen reader menu, hide the keyboard and switch keyboard.

The menu and its lists always work the same way: one finger right or left, next or previous item; one finger up or down, the group (the emoji categories); two fingers down, choose; two fingers up, leave the menu; two fingers right, add to or remove from favourites. Typing a letter also closes the list.

The clipboard remembers what you copy while the braille keyboard is the selected one, only in memory. Lock the orientation keeps the dots as the sensor detected them.

This menu can be changed: in Settings, Braille, «Choose the braille keyboard menu» you remove what you do not use and order the rest. The screen reader menu, dictation, Editing and emoji have their own lessons next.
Whole words

You now know every letter. Next, words: Tiresias says one and you type it letter by letter; each correct letter is spoken. No space is needed at the end. If you make a mistake, it tells you what you typed and the expected letter with its dots, and you carry on from there. Any gesture reminds you of the word and how far you are.\n\nThere is one with ñ, one with an accent, one with a capital and a number: sol, casa, niño, café, Tiresias and 2026.
Free practice

Here you type whatever you like, with nobody correcting you: each letter is spoken as you type it and space says the finished word. With the Enter gesture (by default, two fingers down) you hear everything typed, and delete and delete word work too.\n\nIt is the best way to get going before using it for real. Nothing you type here is saved.
Using it for real

To type with the braille keyboard in any app:

1. Enable it once in the system keyboard settings: «Tiresias braille keyboard». Android warns that a keyboard can see what you type; it is the usual warning for any keyboard.
2. In a text field, switch to it. On Android 11 or later Tiresias does it with the «Braille keyboard» action (put it on a gesture or find it in the actions menu); on earlier versions, the system keyboard list appears.
3. Type. With Tiresias on, the keyboard takes up the whole screen and your fingers reach it directly. When you send or search with Enter (two fingers down), the keyboard hides by itself; to hide it without sending anything, one finger down. It opens again when you touch the field. Two fingers up take you back to the keyboard you had before.

If you prefer it not to hide after sending, in Settings, Braille, turn off «Hide the keyboard after sending or searching».

If something does not respond, both volume keys together remove the braille keyboard and bring back the Tiresias gestures.

Dictate with your voice

Sometimes saying it is faster than typing it. Without leaving the braille keyboard, slide two fingers right (or choose «Dictate» in the keyboard menu) and speak: what you say is typed at the cursor and Tiresias reads it. If the field asks for it, the first letter is a capital, and if the text before does not end in a space, one is added.

To stop it early, repeat the same gesture. It uses Tiresias speech recognition: the one that works without the Internet if you have downloaded its model, or the system one. The first time, Android asks for microphone permission.

Then you carry on typing in braille as usual: you can mix both in the same message.
Move through and correct the text

You do not need to leave the keyboard to review what you have typed.

Three fingers left or right move the cursor and say what it passes over. Three fingers down change what it moves by: characters, words or lines. At the start or the end, it tells you. What you type goes where the cursor is, and delete removes what is before it (to its left): that is how you fix a letter in the middle of a word.

In the keyboard menu, «Editing» has what a text editor has:

Start selecting: from then on, what you move over with the cursor is selected; «Stop selecting» says how many characters you have.
Select all.
Copy and cut the selection; paste what was copied.
Undo and redo.
Go to the start and to the end.
Read the selection.

«Read everything typed», in the same menu, says the whole field. In a password, if Android does not show what you type, Tiresias says «dot» instead of the letters. All of this can be tried in the field of the last lesson.
Emoji: explore, search and favourites

There are two ways to add an emoji, both from the keyboard menu.

Explore: «Emoji» opens the list by group: first your favourites, then your own categories and then the usual ones (faces, gestures, people, hearts, animals, food, activities, travel, objects, symbols and flags). One finger up or down changes group; one finger sideways, emoji; two fingers down type it and the list stays open to add more.

Search: «Search for an emoji» lets you type words of its name in braille, without accents if you like. After each letter, Tiresias says how many there are and the first one; a letter that leaves none is ignored. One finger sideways goes through the results; one finger down starts another word; two fingers left delete a letter; two down type the emoji; two up leave. The names come from the Tiresias emoji base, in your language.

Favourites: in both, two fingers right add the emoji to favourites, and the same gesture removes it.

Your categories: three fingers right save the emoji in one of your categories (Family, Work, whatever you like); if it was already there, they remove it. Categories are created, renamed and deleted in Settings, Braille, «My emoji: favourites and categories», where you can also add emoji by searching for them, remove them, move them from one category to another and order them.

In the practice you search for a real emoji: try adding it to favourites and then choose it with two fingers down.
Type without anyone seeing it

With Tiresias on, the braille keyboard covers the whole app while you type: what you type is not shown on the screen, only a black surface with its name at the top.

If you also turn on the Tiresias screen curtain, the screen goes completely black, without that name, and the keyboard works just the same: the curtain lets your fingers through. That way nobody around you sees what you type or that you are typing.

Remember that what you type is spoken: with headphones, only you hear it. In a password, if Android does not show what you type, Tiresias says «dot» instead of each letter.

Practice: search for an emoji. Type letters of its name in braille, for example hea, for heart. One finger sideways goes through the results; two fingers right, favourite; two left delete a letter; two down choose it. Two up, leave.

The screen reader menu: Tiresias without leaving the keyboard

Three fingers up open the screen reader menu: Tiresias actions you can use while you type, without closing the keyboard. By default: the screen curtain, the time and battery, the notification summary, repeat the last thing, read the clipboard, voice speed and volume, and music (pause and resume). It works the same way as the keyboard menu.

Only actions that say something or change a setting are there: those that open a window or move around the screen do not work with the keyboard on, because the surface would cover them.

To choose it to your liking, in Settings, Braille, «Choose the screen reader menu on the braille keyboard»: check the ones you want (also pitch, punctuation, change voice or language, answer or reject a call…) and order them.

And to have them even closer, any of them can be put directly on a keyboard gesture, in «Braille keyboard gestures»: they are at the end of the list, with «Screen reader» in front. For example, three fingers down for the curtain.
